What We'd Suggest

If it's your first visit and you want the "wow" moment, go Río Celeste in dry season or early/late green season, just know it's about beauty over swimming, and the trail can be slick after rain. If you're here to get in the water and have fun, La Leona or a Rincón-area waterfall trip will feel more rewarding, especially in green season when the rivers are full and the forest is lush.

Because these spots are inland and roads can get rough, most travelers find it easier to go with a driver-guide who knows current trail and water conditions, that day-to-day local knowledge matters more than people expect, since a rainy morning can change which waterfall is worth visiting.

content_block_1:
What a Waterfall & Lunch Half-Day Looks Like

A half-day with a private driver is the easiest way to see a bit of Guanacaste's interior without committing to a full-day excursion. The format is simple: your driver picks you up at your hotel, takes you to a waterfall for a swim and photos, then stops at a good local restaurant for lunch before bringing you home. You set the pace, and there's no shared van, no rigid group schedule, and no waiting on strangers.

Because everything is private, the day flexes around you. If you want an extra half-hour at the falls or a longer, leisurely lunch, that's your call. Guanacaste's dry season runs December through April, which is the most reliable window for clear trails and easy river access.

The Wild Papagayo Recommendation

We arrange these half-days as fully private trips with a local driver who knows the roads and the timing. Pair the waterfall with lunch at a spot we actually trust in the area, and we'll build the route so you're back in time to enjoy the rest of your afternoon at the beach or pool.
content_block_2:
How to Plan It Well

Timing is everything on a half-day. We usually recommend an earlier start so you reach the waterfall before the midday heat and get the best light and cooler water. That also puts you at lunch at a natural hour rather than mid-afternoon when kitchens slow down.

Tell us where you're staying and roughly how much driving you're comfortable with, and we'll match the waterfall and restaurant to keep the day relaxed. For lunch, Guanacaste has genuinely good options like Little Lucha Taqueria and Tropic Tamarindo Costarican Cuisine, and closer to Papagayo you've got spots like Niri Beach Club and Coco's Tiki Bar.

Local Expert Tip
Pack a dry bag with water shoes and a towel and leave them in the vehicle. River rocks near waterfalls are slick, and having grip on your feet turns a cautious wade into a proper swim.
content_block_3:
Our Bottom Line

If you want a genuine taste of Guanacaste beyond the resort without giving up a whole day, a private waterfall-and-lunch half-day is one of the best-value outings we arrange. It's flexible, low-stress, and perfectly doable from the Papagayo area, especially in the December-to-April dry season. Give us your hotel and interests and we'll handle the route, the driver, and the timing.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

How long does the half-day take?

Plan on roughly four to five hours door to door, depending on how far the waterfall is from your hotel and how long you linger over lunch. Because it's fully private, you control the pace and can shorten or extend any stop.

What's the best time of year for a waterfall trip?

The dry season, December through April, is the most reliable window in Guanacaste and Papagayo. Trails are easier and river access is more predictable, though waterfalls can still run strong right after the green season.

Can you handle pickup from the Four Seasons or other Papagayo hotels?

Yes. We arrange private pickups directly from Peninsula Papagayo resorts, including the Four Seasons, as well as hotels across the wider Guanacaste area. Just tell us where you're staying.
travel_tip: Bring small cash in colones for the waterfall entrance and any roadside fruit stands your driver passes -- cards aren't always accepted at rural stops.

title: Río Negro Tubing at Hacienda Guachipelín
excerpt: Ride 5 kilometers of Class II and III rapids on the Río Negro at Hacienda Guachipelín, surrounded by clear water, tropical forest and volcanic scenery.
seo_title_pro: Río Negro Tubing at Hacienda Guachipelín
seo_description: Experience 5 kilometers of Class II and III rapids on the Río Negro at Hacienda Guachipelín near Rincón de la Vieja in Guanacaste.
seo_keywords: Río Negro tubing, Hacienda Guachipelín tubing, Rincón de la Vieja tours, Guanacaste adventure tours, river tubing Costa Rica
image_top_alt: Traveler tubing through a Río Negro rapid at Hotel Hacienda Guachipelín near Rincón de la Vieja
content_block_1:
What Is the Río Negro Tubing Adventure?

The Río Negro Tubing Adventure takes place at Hotel Hacienda Guachipelín in the Rincón de la Vieja area of Guanacaste. This is not a quiet float down a wide river. It is an active journey through approximately 5 kilometers of Class II and III rapids, narrow volcanic canyons and tropical forest.

Each participant travels in an individual river tube designed for moving water. The current carries you through a combination of playful rapids, calmer sections and curves surrounded by rock walls and vegetation. Guides accompany the group, explain the route and help participants navigate the more active sections of the river.

The experience is especially memorable because the Río Negro feels very different from the beaches and resorts of coastal Guanacaste. In one day, travelers can leave the coast behind and enter a greener volcanic landscape near Rincón de la Vieja.

How Intense Are the Class II and III Rapids?

Class II rapids normally involve moving water, small waves and easy-to-see passages. Class III sections are more energetic, with stronger waves, faster turns and more active maneuvering. Conditions can change depending on recent rain and the river level, so the same route may feel different from one visit to another.

You do not need previous tubing experience, but participants should be comfortable in moving water, able to follow instructions and prepared to get completely wet. This is a high-energy adventure rather than a relaxing lazy-river ride.
content_block_2:
What to Expect at Hotel Hacienda Guachipelín

Before entering the river, the activity team provides a safety briefing and the required equipment. Listen carefully to the instructions about body position, holding the tube, approaching rapids and responding if you become separated from it.

The route combines excitement with impressive scenery. Between rapids, take time to notice the forest, volcanic rock formations and clear natural pools along the Río Negro. Water clarity and speed can vary after rainfall, which is normal for a tropical river.

Who Is This Experience Best For?

Río Negro Tubing is a strong choice for adventurous couples, active groups and families with older children who are comfortable around water. It may not be appropriate for very young children, pregnant travelers or guests with certain back, heart, mobility or recent injury concerns.

Minimum ages, weight limits and other participation rules can change according to the operator and river conditions. Confirm every participant's age and any medical considerations before booking.

What Should You Bring?

Wear a swimsuit or quick-drying clothes because you will be completely wet. Secure water shoes or sandals with heel straps are much better than flip-flops. Bring sunscreen, insect repellent, a towel and a complete change of dry clothing.

Leave loose jewelry and valuables at your hotel. A securely mounted waterproof action camera is more practical than holding a phone on the river.

Can You Combine Tubing With Other Activities?

Yes. Hotel Hacienda Guachipelín is known for multi-adventure experiences that may combine river tubing with ziplining, rappelling, horseback riding, lunch, volcanic mud treatments and natural hot springs.

A combination tour is ideal for travelers who want a full day of adventure near Rincón de la Vieja. Those mainly interested in the river should confirm whether a tubing-only option is available on their preferred date.
travel_tip: Wear closed water shoes or secure sandals with heel straps. Flip-flops can come off in the rapids, and ordinary sneakers may remain wet and uncomfortable for the rest of the day.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

Where does the Río Negro Tubing Adventure take place?

It takes place at Hotel Hacienda Guachipelín in Guanacaste, near Rincón de la Vieja National Park and the city of Liberia.

How long is the tubing route?

The river route covers approximately 5 kilometers through a mixture of Class II and III rapids and calmer sections.

Do I need previous tubing or rafting experience?

No previous tubing experience is normally required, but participants should be comfortable in moving water, follow the guides' instructions and be ready for an active adventure.

Is Río Negro Tubing suitable for children?

It can be suitable for older children who meet the operator's requirements and are comfortable in water. Confirm the current minimum age, size restrictions and river conditions before reserving.

Will safety equipment be provided?

The activity operator provides the required river safety equipment and instructions. Participants should use the equipment exactly as directed throughout the experience.

Can the activity be canceled because of rain?

Light rain does not automatically stop a river tour, but heavy rain or unsafe water levels may cause delays, changes or cancellation. Safety decisions are made according to the conditions on the day.

Can I visit Hacienda Guachipelín from Papagayo?

Yes. It is a popular full-day excursion from Papagayo, Playa Hermosa and Playas del Coco. Private transportation makes the day easier and allows time for additional activities at the hacienda.
content_block_3:
Is Río Negro Tubing Worth It?

Yes, especially for travelers who want more than a traditional beach day in Guanacaste. The combination of Class II and III rapids, tropical forest and volcanic canyon scenery makes the Río Negro one of the most exciting tubing experiences near Rincón de la Vieja.

The activity is energetic, wet and occasionally bumpy, which is exactly what many adventure travelers enjoy about it. It also pairs naturally with the zipline, horseback riding and hot springs available at Hotel Hacienda Guachipelín.

Choose this experience when your group is comfortable with moving water and wants a memorable day beyond the resort. Confirm the latest participation requirements and river conditions before booking.

content_block_1:
Are Smaller Tour Companies Better for Adventure Travelers?

For young travelers interested in volcano hikes, rainforest trails and authentic nature experiences, a smaller local tour company can often provide a better experience than a large bus tour.

Large group excursions normally follow a fixed schedule designed for many different ages, interests and fitness levels. A private or small-group experience gives you more time to ask questions, observe wildlife, explore the trail at a comfortable pace and adjust the day around weather conditions.

This does not mean that every small company automatically offers a better tour. The quality of the guide, the itinerary, safety standards and local knowledge are more important than the size of the company.

Before booking, ask whether the experience is completely private, a guaranteed small group or a shared tour that may include a larger number of participants.

What Should You Look for in a Volcano or Rainforest Guide?

A good nature guide should do more than provide transportation and point toward the trail. Look for someone who can explain the wildlife, volcanic activity, forest ecosystem and local history in a natural and engaging way.

Ask whether the guide regularly visits the specific park or reserve included in your tour. Local experience matters because trail conditions, wildlife locations and weather patterns can change throughout the year.

Adventure travelers should also confirm the actual walking distance, elevation, terrain and pace. Words such as easy, moderate and challenging can mean different things to different companies.

If your group wants a more active day, explain that when requesting a quote. A personalized company should be able to recommend a longer trail or combine hiking with waterfalls, tubing, rafting or hot springs.
content_block_2:
Best Volcano and Rainforest Experiences in Guanacaste

Rincón de la Vieja National Park

Rincón de la Vieja is one of the best choices for travelers staying in Guanacaste who want to experience an active volcanic landscape without traveling across the entire country.

Depending on the selected trail and current park conditions, visitors may encounter tropical forest, volcanic steam vents, bubbling mud areas, waterfalls and wildlife. A private guide can help you understand the geothermal landscape while setting a pace that matches your group's fitness level.

This destination works especially well for active travelers who want a genuine hiking experience rather than spending most of the day inside a vehicle.

Sensoria Rainforest

Sensoria offers a completely different landscape. The experience includes a forest trail surrounded by dense vegetation, waterfalls, wildlife and natural thermal pools.

It is a strong option for travelers who want a quieter and more immersive rainforest experience. Because the reserve is located away from the main coastal towns, private transportation and a knowledgeable guide make the logistics much easier.

The approximately 7-kilometer trail provides enough activity for nature lovers while still allowing time to stop for photography, wildlife observation and swimming.

Arenal and La Fortuna

Arenal is one of Costa Rica's most recognized volcano and rainforest destinations. The region offers hanging bridges, waterfalls, wildlife trails, hot springs and views of Arenal Volcano when weather conditions are clear.

Travelers staying in Guanacaste can visit Arenal as a long full-day excursion, but young hikers who want to explore the region in more depth may prefer spending one or two nights in La Fortuna.

If visiting from Papagayo, Playa Hermosa or Playas del Coco, ask for an early departure and a carefully planned itinerary. Trying to include too many attractions in one day can leave very little time to enjoy each location.

What Is Costa Rica Like in August?

August falls during Costa Rica's green season. In Guanacaste and much of the Pacific region, travelers can experience sunny periods, warm temperatures and tropical showers, often later in the day.

The forest is normally greener, waterfalls can be more impressive and wildlife activity may be rewarding. However, trails may also be muddy and rain can occasionally affect road or river conditions.

Starting early is one of the best strategies for volcano hikes and rainforest excursions. Bring lightweight rain protection and choose a company willing to adjust the itinerary when conditions change.

Private Tour or Small Shared Group?

A shared small-group tour can be more affordable and gives travelers an opportunity to meet other people. However, the route and pace still need to accommodate everyone in the group.

A private tour provides more flexibility. You can request a more challenging pace, spend additional time photographing wildlife, leave earlier or combine activities according to your interests.

For young travelers prioritizing adventure over a general sightseeing experience, a private tour is often the closest match to what they are looking for.
travel_tip: Ask for the exact trail name, walking distance and expected pace before booking. A tour described as a volcano hike may sometimes include only a short nature walk unless you request a more active route.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

Are private tours available for solo travelers or couples?

Yes. Many local operators offer private transportation and guiding for solo travelers, couples and small groups. The cost per person is usually lower when more travelers share the vehicle.

Is August a good month for volcano hiking?

August can be a rewarding month because the forests are green and waterfalls may have stronger water flow. Travelers should expect possible rain, muddy trails and occasional itinerary adjustments.

Which volcano is best for travelers staying in Guanacaste?

Rincón de la Vieja is generally the most practical volcanic destination for travelers staying around Papagayo, Playa Hermosa or Playas del Coco. Arenal offers additional attractions but requires a much longer drive.

Do we need a guide for rainforest hiking?

Some trails can be visited independently, but a knowledgeable guide greatly improves wildlife spotting and helps explain the plants, volcanic features and ecosystem that visitors may otherwise overlook.

How small is a small-group tour?

There is no universal definition. Ask the operator for the maximum number of participants. A tour advertised as a small group may still include more people than expected.

Can we combine volcano hiking with another adventure?

Yes. Around Rincón de la Vieja, hiking can often be combined with tubing, ziplining, waterfalls, horseback riding or hot springs. Consider the total activity level before adding several demanding experiences to the same day.

What should we bring for an August rainforest tour?

Bring comfortable hiking shoes, quick-drying clothing, insect repellent, sunscreen, a lightweight rain jacket, a reusable water bottle and a dry change of clothes.

How can we avoid a family-oriented group tour?

Request a private experience or explain that your group prefers an active pace and nature-focused itinerary. Ask whether the tour includes shopping stops, long restaurant stops or activities designed mainly for young children.
content_block_3:
Our Recommendation for Young Adventure Travelers

For travelers based in Guanacaste, we recommend starting with a privately guided hike at Rincón de la Vieja or a full rainforest experience at Sensoria.

Choose Rincón de la Vieja when volcanic landscapes, geothermal activity and active hiking are your priorities. Choose Sensoria when you want dense rainforest, waterfalls, wildlife and thermal pools in a more remote natural setting.

If your itinerary includes La Fortuna, add Arenal hanging bridges, a waterfall or a dedicated volcano trail rather than trying to experience the entire region during one rushed day trip from the coast.

When contacting a company, be specific about your ages, fitness level and preferred pace. Mention that you want an authentic adventure rather than a general family excursion. This allows the guide to design a day that feels personal instead of following a standard itinerary.

Wild Papagayo specializes in private transportation and personalized nature experiences from the Papagayo and Guanacaste area. Each itinerary can be adjusted according to the group's interests, travel dates and desired activity level.

title: Bat Islands, Costa Rica: A Remote Guanacaste Adventure
excerpt: Far beyond Guanacaste’s resort beaches, the Bat Islands reveal a remote protected seascape of rocky islets, open Pacific water and remarkable marine life.
seo_title_pro: Bat Islands, Costa Rica: Guanacaste Travel Guide
seo_description: Discover Costa Rica’s Bat Islands, a remote Guanacaste archipelago known for protected waters, dramatic scenery and exceptional marine life.
seo_keywords: Bat Islands Costa Rica, Islas Murciélago Guanacaste, Guanacaste marine tours, Costa Rica diving, remote Costa Rica islands
image_top_alt: Natural rock arch rising above the Pacific Ocean at the Bat Islands in Guanacaste, Costa Rica.
content_block_1:
What Are the Bat Islands?

The Bat Islands, known locally as Islas Murciélago, are a remote archipelago off the Santa Elena Peninsula in northern Guanacaste. They form part of the protected marine sector of the Guanacaste Conservation Area and include five islands and ten smaller islets.

This is a very different side of Guanacaste from the beach towns and resorts farther south. The landscape is wild and exposed, with rocky islands, open Pacific water and very little development. The sense of distance is part of what makes the destination memorable.

The protected waters support coral communities and a wide variety of marine life. Depending on the season and conditions, visitors may encounter rays, large schools of fish, dolphins, turtles and other ocean species. Wildlife sightings are never guaranteed, but the area is recognized for its exceptional biodiversity.

Why Are the Bat Islands So Famous?

The archipelago is best known internationally as an advanced scuba-diving destination. San Pedrillo Islet is particularly associated with sightings of large marine animals, including bull sharks and giant manta rays.

That reputation should not make the experience sound like a casual beginner activity. The Bat Islands are remote, and conditions can include wind, current, cooler water and limited visibility. Certified divers should choose an experienced, properly authorized operator and confirm whether the planned sites match their certification and recent experience.

Travelers who do not dive may still appreciate the archipelago through an authorized recreational boat experience when access, weather and ocean conditions allow. However, this is not a conventional beach-hopping destination, and landing on protected islands may be restricted.
content_block_2:
What Is the Journey Like?

Reaching the Bat Islands requires a substantial boat journey into the northern Pacific. Common departure areas can include Cuajiniquil, Playas del Coco, Playa Hermosa or other authorized coastal points, depending on the operator and itinerary.

The ride is part of the experience, with views of the Guanacaste coastline and the rugged Santa Elena Peninsula. It can also feel long or rough when winds increase, so travelers who are sensitive to motion should discuss conditions with the operator before departure.

Because the destination lies inside a protected marine area, visits are regulated. Reservations, entrance authorization, boat documentation and activity limits may apply. These rules can change, so the operator should confirm the current requirements before the trip.

Who Will Enjoy This Experience Most?

The Bat Islands are best suited to adventurous travelers who value remote nature, marine conservation and an uncrowded setting more than resort-style comfort.

Experienced certified divers are the travelers most likely to experience the area's famous underwater sites. Nature lovers may also enjoy a permitted recreational boat visit focused on coastal scenery and wildlife observation.

This destination may not be the best choice for travelers seeking a short, calm cruise, guaranteed wildlife sightings or easy beach access. Families with very young children and anyone uncomfortable with long boat rides should compare it with gentler marine excursions closer to the Gulf of Papagayo.

How Does Weather Affect the Trip?

Ocean conditions matter more than the calendar alone. Strong winds, waves or poor visibility can change the route or cause a trip to be postponed. The captain and authorized operator should make the final decision based on conditions that day.

Travelers should keep the day flexible and avoid planning an important flight or fixed activity immediately afterward. A remote marine excursion works best when there is room in the itinerary for weather-related changes.

What Should You Bring?

Bring sun protection, a hat that can be secured, a light long-sleeved layer, a reusable water bottle and any medication normally used for motion sensitivity. Keep electronics and important documents in a waterproof pouch.

For any organized marine activity, follow the operator's safety briefing and use the equipment they provide. Do not touch, feed or chase wildlife, and never remove coral, shells, rocks or other natural material from the protected area.
travel_tip: Ask the operator to confirm the exact departure point, total time on the boat, current marine access rules and expected ocean conditions before reserving. The Bat Islands are remote, so those details matter more than the advertised tour length alone.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

Where are the Bat Islands located?

They are off the Santa Elena Peninsula in northern Guanacaste and form part of the protected marine sector of the Guanacaste Conservation Area.

How many islands are in the archipelago?

The Bat Islands archipelago includes five islands and ten smaller islets.

Are the Bat Islands only for scuba divers?

No, but the destination is best known for advanced scuba diving. Authorized recreational boat visits may also be possible when regulations and ocean conditions allow.

Can beginners dive at the Bat Islands?

The area is generally considered better suited to experienced certified divers because conditions can include current, wind, cooler water and remote dive sites. Travelers should discuss certification and recent experience with an authorized operator.

Are bull shark sightings guaranteed?

No. The area is known for bull sharks and other large marine animals, but wildlife encounters can never be guaranteed.

Can visitors walk on the islands?

Landing and access may be restricted because the archipelago is protected. Visitors should follow the current instructions issued by the conservation authority and their authorized operator.

Where do Bat Islands trips depart from?

Departure points vary. Common access areas can include Cuajiniquil, Playas del Coco and Playa Hermosa, but travelers should confirm the exact marina or beach before booking.

Can weather cancel the trip?

Yes. Strong winds, waves or other unsafe marine conditions may change or cancel the excursion. The captain should make the final navigation decision.
content_block_3:
Are the Bat Islands Worth Visiting?

For the right traveler, yes. The Bat Islands offer a rare opportunity to experience a remote and highly protected part of northern Guanacaste, far from the region's busier beaches and resort areas.

The destination is especially rewarding for experienced divers, marine-life enthusiasts and travelers who understand that wild places come with changing conditions and no guaranteed sightings.

Choose this experience for its isolation, conservation value and dramatic Pacific scenery—not because you expect a simple beach day. A responsible operator, flexible schedule and realistic expectations are essential for enjoying the journey.

title: Costa Rica’s UNESCO World Heritage: Land, Ocean and Culture
excerpt: Costa Rica’s four UNESCO World Heritage properties protect extraordinary forests, marine ecosystems, wildlife and an important part of the country’s pre-Columbian history.
seo_title_pro: Costa Rica’s Four UNESCO World Heritage Sites
seo_description: Explore Costa Rica’s four UNESCO World Heritage properties and how they protect forests, oceans, biodiversity and pre-Columbian culture.
seo_keywords: Costa Rica UNESCO sites, Costa Rica World Heritage, Guanacaste Conservation Area, Cocos Island, Diquís stone spheres
image_top_alt: Historic La Casona building at Santa Rosa National Park in the Guanacaste Conservation Area, Costa Rica.
content_block_1:
Why World Heritage Matters in Costa Rica

Costa Rica is internationally recognized for its biodiversity, protected landscapes and strong connection between nature and tourism. One of the clearest examples is the country’s four properties inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Three of these properties are recognized for their natural importance, while one protects an exceptional part of Costa Rica’s pre-Columbian cultural history. Together, they represent tropical forests, volcanic landscapes, remote marine ecosystems, mountain habitats and archaeological sites.

World Heritage recognition is more than an international title. It creates a responsibility to protect places considered valuable not only to Costa Rica, but to humanity as a whole.

Costa Rica’s Four UNESCO World Heritage Properties

1. Area de Conservación Guanacaste

Located in northwestern Costa Rica, the Area de Conservación Guanacaste protects an extraordinary connection between land and ocean. Its ecosystems extend from the Pacific coast through tropical dry forest, volcanic mountains and humid forests toward the Caribbean lowlands.

The protected area includes beaches, forests, wetlands, rivers, islands and marine environments. Rincón de la Vieja is part of this broader conservation landscape, making it especially relevant to travelers exploring Guanacaste.

2. Cocos Island National Park

Cocos Island National Park protects one of Costa Rica’s most remote natural treasures. Located far from the Pacific mainland, the property includes a forest-covered oceanic island and an extensive protected marine environment.

Its waters are internationally known for marine biodiversity and encounters with large ocean species. Because of its isolation and environmental importance, Cocos Island is not a conventional beach destination and requires carefully regulated access.
content_block_2:
3. Talamanca Range–La Amistad Reserves and La Amistad National Park

This transboundary World Heritage property extends across Costa Rica and Panama. It protects large areas of tropical rainforest, cloud forest, high mountains and habitats containing remarkable biological diversity.

The Talamanca Mountains also hold deep cultural importance. Indigenous communities have lived within and around this region for generations, creating a connection between environmental protection, traditional knowledge and human history.

4. Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements With Stone Spheres of the Diquís

Costa Rica’s cultural World Heritage property includes four archaeological sites in the Diquís Delta: Finca 6, Batambal, El Silencio and Grijalba-2.

These sites preserve evidence of complex pre-Columbian societies, including settlement areas, artificial mounds, paved spaces, burial sites and the famous stone spheres of southern Costa Rica.

The spheres are admired for their size, craftsmanship and remarkably rounded form. Many questions about their original purpose and production remain unanswered, adding to their cultural and archaeological significance.

Three Natural Properties and One Cultural Property

The World Heritage List shows that Costa Rica’s identity is not based on nature alone. Its three natural properties protect biodiversity and major ecosystems, while the Diquís archaeological sites preserve evidence of the people who shaped the country long before the modern era.

This combination gives travelers a more complete understanding of Costa Rica. National parks, forests and marine reserves are essential, but archaeological heritage, local communities and cultural history also deserve protection and respect.

How Conservation Supports Costa Rica’s Tourism Identity

Costa Rica’s international tourism reputation depends heavily on healthy forests, clean water, wildlife and protected landscapes. Visitors travel to the country to experience volcanoes, rainforests, beaches, marine life and living ecosystems.

Protecting these places helps preserve the experiences travelers come to enjoy. It also creates opportunities for local guides, conservation programs, researchers and communities connected to responsible tourism.

However, recognition can also bring pressure. Increased visitation must be managed carefully so that tourism does not damage the natural or cultural values that made these places exceptional.
travel_tip: Do not treat World Heritage properties as a checklist to complete in one vacation. Choose one region, learn why it is protected and support authorized guides and services that follow conservation rules.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

How many UNESCO World Heritage properties does Costa Rica have?

Costa Rica currently has four properties inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

How many are natural World Heritage properties?

Three are classified as natural properties: Area de Conservación Guanacaste, Cocos Island National Park and Talamanca Range–La Amistad Reserves and La Amistad National Park.

What is Costa Rica’s cultural World Heritage property?

It is the Precolumbian Chiefdom Settlements with Stone Spheres of the Diquís, composed of four archaeological sites in southern Costa Rica.

Is Rincón de la Vieja part of a World Heritage property?

Yes. Rincón de la Vieja forms part of the wider Area de Conservación Guanacaste World Heritage property.

Can tourists visit all four properties?

Access varies significantly. Some areas have established visitor trails and facilities, while remote or sensitive locations may require special planning, authorized operators or regulated access.

Is Cocos Island easy to visit from Guanacaste?

No. Cocos Island is located far offshore and is not a standard day trip from Guanacaste. Visiting requires specialized planning and authorized marine transportation.

Why are the Diquís stone spheres important?

They form part of archaeological settlements that demonstrate the organization, craftsmanship and social complexity of pre-Columbian societies in southern Costa Rica.

How can travelers support conservation?

Travelers can use authorized guides, follow park rules, avoid disturbing wildlife, remain on established trails, reduce waste and respect archaeological and cultural sites.
content_block_3:
Protecting More Than Beautiful Scenery

Costa Rica’s four World Heritage properties show that environmental and cultural protection can be central to a country’s identity.

Area de Conservación Guanacaste connects forests, volcanoes and marine environments. Cocos Island protects an exceptional oceanic ecosystem. La Amistad preserves one of Central America’s most important mountain and rainforest landscapes. The Diquís sites protect the legacy of sophisticated pre-Columbian communities.

These places are not valuable only because they are beautiful or attractive to travelers. They preserve biodiversity, scientific knowledge, cultural memory and natural processes that cannot easily be replaced.

Responsible tourism begins by understanding that every protected destination is also a living ecosystem or cultural landscape. Visiting with respect helps Costa Rica continue protecting its land, ocean and heritage for future generations.

title: Can You Bring a Phone on Costa Rica Adventure Tours?
excerpt: Wondering where to keep your phone, towels and valuables during Costa Rica adventure tours? Here is what to expect on rafting, ziplining, ATV and catamaran excursions.
seo_title_pro: Can You Bring a Phone on Costa Rica Adventure Tours?
seo_description: Learn where to store phones, towels and valuables during rafting, ziplining, ATV and catamaran tours in Costa Rica, with practical safety tips.
seo_keywords: phone on Costa Rica tours, Costa Rica rafting what to bring, zipline phone rules, ATV tour packing list, catamaran dry bag
image_top_alt: Alt text: Green waterproof phone pouch with a clear touchscreen window and secure locking clips.
content_block_1:
Should You Bring Your Phone on an Adventure Tour?

You can bring your phone to the tour meeting point, but that does not mean you should carry it during every activity. Rafting, ziplining, ATV riding and catamaran cruises have very different rules and levels of water exposure.

The safest general plan is to bring only essential items and ask the operator where personal belongings will be stored before the activity begins. Some companies provide lockers, changing rooms, secure vehicle storage or a designated dry bag. Others require guests to leave phones, backpacks and loose items behind.

Do not depend only on a waterproof phone pouch. A pouch may protect a device from splashes, but it can still be lost, damaged or prohibited if it interferes with safety equipment or movement.

Around-the-neck phone pouch is not the best default choice for rafting or ziplining. Even when the pouch is waterproof, the operator may consider it a loose or distracting object. Only carry it when the guide specifically confirms that it is permitted.

The Best General Protocol

Before leaving your hotel, place your phone, wallet, documents and dry clothing inside one small backpack or dry bag. When you arrive, ask whether that bag will remain in a locker, transportation vehicle, changing area or secure storage location.

Carry only the items approved by the guide during the active portion of the tour. The operator's instructions should always take priority over advice from social media, previous travelers or product advertising.

It is also helpful to ask whether the company offers professional photographs. On rafting and zipline tours, purchasing the operator's photos can be easier and safer than trying to carry a phone throughout the experience.
content_block_2:
What to Do With Your Phone During Whitewater Rafting

For whitewater rafting, we recommend leaving your regular phone, wallet and towel in the storage location designated by the operator. Bring clothing that can get completely wet and keep a dry change of clothes ready for after the river.

Some rafting companies allow securely mounted action cameras, while others restrict all personal cameras. Rules can also change according to the river, rapid classification and water conditions.

Do not assume that a waterproof backpack can travel inside the raft. A large personal bag may move around, become difficult to secure or interfere with the space needed by participants and guides. Ask whether the operator provides a secured river dry bag for essential items.

Your quick-dry towel should normally remain with your dry clothes rather than travel down the river. You will not need it while rafting, and keeping it dry makes it useful when the activity ends.

What to Do With Your Phone While Ziplining

Zipline rules are usually stricter because participants must keep their hands free and avoid objects that could fall. Some Costa Rica zipline operators do not allow cell phones, cameras, bags, hats or other loose items during the activity.

Use the company's lockers or secure storage when available. A phone inside an ordinary pocket is not necessarily permitted, even if the pocket has a zipper.

Ask whether the operator has a professional photography service or allows an approved, securely mounted action camera. Never assume that a handheld phone, selfie stick or neck pouch will be accepted.

What to Do With Your Phone on an ATV Tour

A small waterproof or dust-resistant bag may be useful during an ATV excursion, but it must be stored according to the guide's instructions. Roads and trails can be wet, dusty, muddy and uneven.

Keep the phone stored while the ATV is moving. Only take it out after the group has stopped in an approved location and the guide confirms it is safe to do so.

A waterproof case protects against rain and mud, but it does not protect a phone from falling, vibration or impact. Avoid carrying unnecessary valuables during the ride.

What to Bring on a Catamaran

A catamaran is normally the activity where a waterproof phone pouch or small dry bag is most useful. You may want your phone for photographs, but it should remain protected from sea spray, wet surfaces and swimming stops.

Keep the pouch secured and avoid placing the phone on seats, railings or the edge of the boat. For swimming or snorkeling, leave it aboard unless the crew confirms that carrying it in the water is appropriate.

Bring a quick-dry towel, sunscreen, a hat and dry clothing if recommended by the operator. Some catamarans provide towels, while others expect passengers to bring their own, so confirm this before departure.
travel_tip: Send each tour company one message before your trip asking three questions: Are phones allowed during the activity, is secure storage provided and are professional photos available? The answers may be different for every tour.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

Can I wear a waterproof phone pouch around my neck while rafting?

Do not assume that it is allowed. Some operators prohibit personal items that could interfere with movement or safety equipment. Ask the rafting company directly and leave the phone in secure storage when the answer is unclear.

Can I bring a waterproof backpack inside the raft?

Only when the operator approves it. Many companies prefer to secure essential items in their own dry bag or leave personal backpacks at the operations center, in a locker or inside the transportation vehicle.

Should I bring a towel while rafting?

Bring a small quick-dry towel, but leave it with your dry clothes during the river portion. It is more useful after the activity than inside the raft.

Are phones allowed while ziplining?

Policies vary, but many zipline operators prohibit cell phones, cameras and loose objects. Use lockers or the company's photography service when available.

Can I take photographs during an ATV tour?

Keep the phone stored while the ATV is moving. Photographs should only be taken at designated stops after following the guide's instructions.

Should I bring a dry bag on a catamaran?

Yes, a small dry bag can be useful for protecting electronics, clothing and personal items from spray. Keep it closed and stored securely while the boat is moving.

What valuables should I leave at the hotel?

Leave passports, expensive jewelry, unnecessary cards and large amounts of cash in your hotel safe. Carry only what you genuinely need for the excursion.

What happens if the tour does not provide lockers?

Ask whether belongings remain inside the transportation vehicle or at the operations center. Do not leave valuables unattended without first understanding the company's storage procedure.
content_block_3:
Our Recommendation for Your Four Excursions

For whitewater rafting, bring almost nothing onto the river. Leave your phone, towel and dry clothing in the storage area identified by the operator. Carry an action camera only when the company explicitly permits it.

For ziplining, expect strict rules about cell phones, cameras, bags and loose objects. Plan to use a locker or professional photography service.

For the ATV tour, protect your phone from rain, dust and mud, but keep it stored while the vehicle is moving. Use it only during approved stops.

For the catamaran, a small dry bag and waterproof phone pouch are more practical. Even then, keep electronics protected and securely stored when swimming or moving around the boat.

You do not need to arrive with nothing at all. Bring a compact bag with a quick-dry towel, dry clothes, sunscreen and essential personal items, then follow the storage procedure provided by each company.

title: Costa Rica Place Names Travelers Often Get Wrong
excerpt: Tourism, social media and online maps can popularize names that differ from Costa Rica’s official cartography. Discover why correct place names matter.
seo_title_pro: Costa Rica Place Names Travelers Often Get Wrong
seo_description: Learn why popular island and coastal names in Costa Rica may differ from official cartography, and how travelers can verify the correct names.
seo_keywords: Costa Rica place names, Costa Rica islands, Costa Rica geography, official maps Costa Rica, geographic names Costa Rica
image_top_alt: Large rocky sea stack rising from the blue Pacific Ocean along the Costa Rican coast.
content_block_1:
Why Costa Rica’s Geographic Names Matter

Costa Rica is known for volcanoes, beaches, islands, rivers, rainforests and an extraordinary variety of natural landscapes. Many of these places are promoted internationally through travel websites, social media, navigation applications and tour advertisements.

However, the name travelers see online is not always the same name used in Costa Rica’s official cartography. Some destinations are marketed under an easier nickname, an English translation, a shortened version or a name created through local and tourism use.

This does not necessarily mean that travelers or tourism businesses are intentionally sharing false information. Place names naturally evolve, and a popular name may become so widely recognized that it feels official. The problem begins when the popular name completely replaces the historical or cartographic name without explanation.

Geographic names are part of Costa Rica’s cultural heritage. They can preserve indigenous words, historical events, local traditions, references to plants and animals, or descriptions of the landscape itself.

Who Protects Costa Rica’s Official Place Names?

Costa Rica created the National Nomenclature Commission through Law No. 3535 of August 3, 1965. One of its responsibilities is to help preserve the traditional and native names of Costa Rican geography.

The National Geographic Institute is the country’s official cartographic authority. Its geographic information standards distinguish between an official or generally accepted name and a nonofficial name used without formal authorization from the State.

This distinction is important for maps, public signs, tourism information, emergency response, research and historical preservation. When everyone uses completely different names for the same location, confusion becomes more likely.
content_block_2:
Popular Names and Official Cartography Are Not Always the Same

A tourism name can still be useful. Travelers often need a familiar term to find an excursion, communicate with a driver or search for a destination online. The goal is not to remove every popular name, but to explain how it relates to the official geography.

Isla Tortuga, Tolinga and the Islas Tortugas

One of the clearest examples is the destination commonly marketed as Isla Tortuga. Most visitors use this name when searching for boat tours in the Gulf of Nicoya.

Official geographic records identify Tolinga as part of the Islas Tortugas group and also list Alcatraz as another island within that group. This means that the tourism expression Isla Tortuga does not tell the complete geographic story.

A responsible travel article can still use Isla Tortuga because travelers recognize it, but it should also explain that the main island is Tolinga and that the area includes additional islands and islets.

Bat Islands and the Murciélago Archipelago

International travelers commonly search for Bat Islands, especially when researching diving and marine experiences in northern Guanacaste.

Official conservation sources use Spanish forms such as Archipiélago Islas Murciélago and Archipiélago de las Islas Murciélago. The protected archipelago is associated with the Santa Elena Peninsula and forms part of the marine sector of the Guanacaste Conservation Area.

The English name Bat Islands is useful for tourism and international communication, but including the Spanish geographic name helps visitors understand the destination’s local identity.

The Name May Not Be the Only Error

Sometimes the confusion is not only about the name. A feature described online as an island may officially be classified as an islet, rock, point, bay or coastal formation.

These words describe different geographic features. An island is land surrounded by water, while a point is connected to the mainland. An islet is generally smaller than an island, and a rock may not support the same vegetation or terrain.

From a tourism perspective, the difference may appear minor. From a cartographic, environmental and cultural perspective, it matters. Correct classification helps people understand the real landscape and reduces the spread of inaccurate information.

How Online Maps Can Spread Alternative Names

Collaborative maps and social platforms are extremely useful for travelers, but their place labels may be submitted by businesses or individual users. A scenic viewpoint, rock formation or swimming area can receive an informal name that quickly becomes popular.

Once travel blogs, photographs and tour companies repeat that name, search engines may begin presenting it as the main identification for the location. Visitors then repeat it in reviews and social posts, creating a cycle in which the unofficial name becomes more visible than the cartographic one.

This is why the first search result should not always be treated as the final authority on Costa Rican geography.

How Travelers Can Verify a Place Name

Begin by comparing several sources. Look at information from the National Geographic Institute, the National Territorial Information System, national parks, conservation areas, municipalities and other Costa Rican government institutions.

When the sources use different versions, do not immediately assume that one is wrong. The difference may reflect a tourism name, local name, historic name, official name or a label used at a different map scale.

A helpful way to write the destination is to include both forms. For example, an article can introduce a place as Tolinga, commonly promoted as Isla Tortuga, or the Murciélago Archipelago, internationally known as the Bat Islands.
travel_tip: When a boat captain, local guide and online map use different names, save the location coordinates and ask for the official or traditional Spanish name. This prevents confusion without dismissing the name used by local residents.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

Are popular tourism names always incorrect?

No. A popular name may be useful, historically established or widely recognized by local residents. It simply may not match the name recorded in official cartography.

Is Isla Tortuga the official name of the island?

Isla Tortuga is the name most travelers and tour companies use. Official geographic records identify Tolinga within the Islas Tortugas group and also list Alcatraz as part of that island group.

Are the Bat Islands a real destination?

Yes. Bat Islands is the English tourism name for the protected Murciélago archipelago in northern Guanacaste. The issue is not whether the destination exists, but how its Spanish geographic name is written and understood.

Why do Google Maps and official maps sometimes disagree?

Collaborative platforms may include names submitted by users or businesses, while official maps follow national cartographic standards and institutional records.

Can a place have more than one valid name?

Yes. A location may have an official name, traditional name, local nickname, historical name and translated tourism name. Good travel information explains the relationship between them.

Why does the geographic classification matter?

Calling a point an island or a rock an islet changes how people understand the landscape. Accurate classifications also support mapping, navigation, conservation and emergency planning.

Where can travelers verify Costa Rican place names?

Travelers can consult the National Geographic Institute, the National Territorial Information System, official conservation-area websites and government maps.

Should tourism companies stop using familiar names?

Not necessarily. Familiar names help travelers find destinations. The most responsible approach is to mention the recognized tourism name together with the official or traditional name.
content_block_3:
Traveling With Greater Respect for Costa Rica

Learning the correct name of a destination is more than a geography lesson. It is a way to recognize Costa Rica’s history, culture and local knowledge.

Travelers do not need to memorize every official island, rock or coastal point. What matters is remaining curious and understanding that the label shown on a tourism advertisement may represent only one version of the place’s identity.

Travel writers and tour companies also have an important role. By checking official sources and explaining alternative names, they can create content that is both useful for international visitors and respectful of Costa Rica’s geographic heritage.

The next time two maps use different names, treat the difference as an invitation to learn more. Behind every name there may be a story about local communities, wildlife, navigation, history or the physical landscape itself.

title: How Many Beaches Does Costa Rica Really Have?
excerpt: Costa Rica has hundreds of named beaches across the Pacific and Caribbean. Discover why counting them is complicated and what official maps reveal.
seo_title_pro: How Many Beaches Does Costa Rica Really Have?
seo_description: Explore Costa Rica’s coastal geography, official beach names and hidden shores across Guanacaste, the Pacific and the Caribbean.
seo_keywords: Costa Rica beaches, official beaches Costa Rica, Guanacaste beaches, Costa Rica coastal geography, hidden beaches Costa Rica
image_top_alt: Vibrant sunset over a Costa Rican beach with orange clouds, gentle waves and a rocky silhouette offshore.
content_block_1:
How Many Beaches Does Costa Rica Have?

Costa Rica has hundreds of beaches distributed along the Pacific Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, bays, gulfs, islands, estuaries, wetlands and protected coastal areas.

However, answering exactly how many beaches the country has is more complicated than adding the names found on a tourism website or navigation application.

Official cartography may recognize a beach under a different name from the one used by local residents, hotels or tour companies. Some smaller coastal sections may not have an individually registered name, while others may have received a popular name after the original map was produced.

For this reason, a list based on official maps should be understood as a geographic inventory rather than a final count of every place people currently call a beach.

A Country Between Two Coasts

Costa Rica has coastlines on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. Although the country is relatively small, its coastal geography is remarkably diverse.

Travelers can encounter wide open-ocean beaches, protected bays, volcanic shorelines, coral-influenced Caribbean beaches, mangrove channels, island beaches and long stretches of sand beside wetlands and river mouths.

This diversity means that two Costa Rican beaches located only a few hours apart can have completely different landscapes, wave conditions, ecosystems and travel experiences.
content_block_2:
Why Are More Named Beaches Found on the Pacific Coast?

Most of the named beaches included in traditional Costa Rican cartography are located along the Pacific coast. This side of the country has a highly irregular shoreline with peninsulas, gulfs, bays, islands and many smaller coastal sections.

The Pacific inventory includes beaches around Bahía de Salinas, the Gulf of Santa Elena, the Gulf of Papagayo, the Nicoya Peninsula, the Gulf of Nicoya, the Central Pacific, the Osa Peninsula and Golfo Dulce.

By comparison, parts of the Caribbean coastline consist of longer continuous stretches of beach. Some coastal sections have historically been identified using nearby rivers, towns or geographic reference points instead of separate beach names.

Guanacaste Has More Than Famous Resort Beaches

International visitors often recognize names such as Playas del Coco, Playa Hermosa, Playa Panamá, Tamarindo, Conchal and Sámara. These are only a small part of Guanacaste’s coastal geography.

Northern Guanacaste includes remote beaches around Bahía de Salinas, the Santa Elena Peninsula and Santa Rosa National Park. The Gulf of Papagayo and Bahía Culebra contain additional beaches hidden between headlands, protected bays and undeveloped coastal areas.

Some can be reached by paved road, while others may require a four-wheel-drive vehicle, boat transportation, a national park entrance or permission to cross private property. A beach appearing on a map does not automatically mean it has easy or public road access.

Beaches Around the Gulf of Papagayo

The wider Papagayo region includes recognized beaches such as Playa Cabuyal, Playa Iguanita, Playa Panamá, Playa Hermosa, Playas del Coco and Playa Ocotal.

There are also smaller beaches and coves whose names are less familiar to international travelers. These places demonstrate why Papagayo should not be viewed as a single beach, but as a coastal region formed by bays, peninsulas and many individual shorelines.

Tourism Names and Official Names May Differ

A beach can have an official cartographic name and still be better known under a tourism or commercial name. The familiar name may come from a nearby hotel, community, marina, property or local tradition.

This does not always make the popular name wrong. It simply means that travelers may encounter different names for the same coastal area when comparing road signs, online maps, local directions and official cartography.

A responsible travel guide should mention both versions when the difference could cause confusion. This helps visitors find the destination while also preserving its geographic and cultural identity.

Many Beaches Are Inside Protected Areas

Some of Costa Rica’s most important beaches lie within national parks, wildlife refuges, wetlands and biological reserves.

Examples include beaches associated with Santa Rosa National Park, Marino Las Baulas National Park, Ostional Wildlife Refuge, Manuel Antonio National Park, Marino Ballena National Park, Corcovado National Park, Tortuguero National Park and Cahuita National Park.

These beaches are not protected only for their scenery. They may support sea turtle nesting, coastal forests, coral ecosystems, mangroves, marine wildlife and important bird habitats.

Access rules can include entrance fees, operating hours, seasonal restrictions and limits on food, pets, vehicles or nighttime visitation. Travelers should check current rules before visiting.

What About Hidden and Remote Beaches?

A beach appearing in official cartography may not have tourism services, lifeguards, restrooms, restaurants or reliable phone coverage.

Remote locations can involve river crossings, rough roads, long walks, changing tides or limited access through protected and privately managed land. Some are better explored with a local guide or licensed boat operator.

Travelers should never assume that a beach is safe for swimming simply because it looks calm. Waves, currents, submerged rocks and rapidly changing tides can affect even beautiful and apparently protected shores.
travel_tip: Before driving to a remote beach, ask a local guide about road access, tides and public entry. A map pin may show the location accurately without showing a locked gate, river crossing or seasonal road condition.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

How many official beaches are there in Costa Rica?

There is no simple permanent number. Cartographic inventories contain hundreds of named coastal areas, but the total can vary according to map scale, classification, updated names and whether long coastal sections are counted as one beach or several.

Does Costa Rica have more Pacific or Caribbean beaches?

Traditional geographic inventories include substantially more individually named beaches on the Pacific side, partly because its coastline contains more bays, gulfs, peninsulas and islands.

Are all beaches in Costa Rica public?

Costa Rica’s maritime zone generally protects public use of the shoreline, but reaching a beach can still be complicated when there is no public road, when access crosses private land or when the beach lies inside a protected area.

Why does a beach have different names on different maps?

A place may have an official cartographic name, a traditional local name and a commercial tourism name. Online mapping platforms may also include names contributed by users or businesses.

Which Guanacaste beaches are easiest for first-time visitors?

Playas del Coco, Playa Hermosa, Playa Panamá, Playa Ocotal, Playa Conchal, Tamarindo and Sámara are among the more accessible options with nearby services and established tourism infrastructure.

Are remote beaches safe for swimming?

Not automatically. Remote beaches may have strong currents, waves, rocks or no lifeguards. Ask locally about conditions and remain out of the water when you are uncertain.

Can travelers visit beaches inside national parks?

Many can be visited during established park hours, but regulations vary. Some locations require advance reservations, entrance fees or authorized transportation.

Where can travelers verify official beach names?

Official geographic information can be checked through Costa Rica’s National Geographic Institute, the National Territorial Information System and the websites of national parks and conservation areas.
content_block_3:
Costa Rica’s Coast Is More Than a Beach Checklist

Costa Rica’s coastline cannot be understood only through its most famous tourism destinations. It includes hundreds of named and unnamed shores connected to islands, wetlands, forests, protected bays and remote national parks.

The official name of a beach is part of the country’s geographic heritage, but local and tourism names also help tell the story of how coastal communities and travel destinations have developed.

For visitors, the most useful approach is not trying to visit as many beaches as possible. Choose a region, learn about its geography and spend enough time to understand how each beach differs in access, wildlife, waves and atmosphere.

In Guanacaste alone, travelers can move from developed beach towns to quiet bays and remote protected shores. That variety is one of the reasons Costa Rica’s coast remains so rewarding to explore.

title: La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo Without the Monkey Trail
excerpt: Driving from La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo? Learn how to avoid Route 911, choose the paved route through Guanacaste and decide between driving or hiring a private transfer.
seo_title_pro: La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo Without Route 911
seo_description: Learn the paved route from La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo, how to avoid the Monkey Trail and whether driving or hiring a private transfer is best.
seo_keywords: La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo, avoid Monkey Trail Costa Rica, Route 911 Costa Rica, Playa Flamingo driving route, Costa Rica private driver
image_top_alt: Arenal Volcano rising above lush green rainforest and farmland near La Fortuna, Costa Rica.
content_block_1:
Can You Drive From La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo Without Route 911?

Yes. You can drive from La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo without using Route 911, commonly called the Monkey Trail.

The usual paved route is longer than the shortcut suggested by some navigation applications, but it avoids the river crossings and narrow mountain section associated with the Monkey Trail.

From La Fortuna, follow Route 142 around Lake Arenal toward Nuevo Arenal, Tilarán and Cañas. From Cañas, join Route 1 and travel north toward Liberia. Continue onto Route 21, then turn toward Belén de Carrillo.

From Belén, take Route 155 toward Huacas. At Huacas, continue on Route 180 toward Brasilito and then follow the coastal road to Playa Flamingo.

The complete route can be summarized as:

La Fortuna → Route 142 → Tilarán → Cañas → Route 1 → Liberia → Route 21 → Belén → Route 155 → Huacas → Route 180 → Brasilito → Playa Flamingo.

How Do You Stop Waze From Choosing the Monkey Trail?

Waze may select Route 911 because it appears shorter. To guide the application toward the paved route, add several intermediate stops instead of entering only Playa Flamingo as the final destination.

Useful waypoints include Cañas, Liberia, Belén de Carrillo, Huacas and Brasilito. Before leaving, review the entire route and confirm that it does not turn from Sardinal toward Potrero on Route 911.

Do not follow a navigation application blindly when it suggests an unfamiliar shortcut. Costa Rican travel times depend on road curves, weather, traffic, construction and the condition of smaller roads.
content_block_2:
Why Do Some Travelers Avoid the Monkey Trail?

Route 911 connects the Sardinal area with Potrero and nearby beach communities. It can save time, but parts of the road are narrow, steep, winding and without shoulders, painted lines or streetlights.

The route is also known for river crossings. Water depth changes according to recent rainfall, and conditions can be less predictable during Costa Rica’s green season.

A private bridge on the Congo Trail property may allow drivers to bypass the main river crossing for a fee during its operating hours. However, travelers who do not want any part of the Route 911 experience should use the longer route through Belén, Huacas and Brasilito.

In July, we would not recommend choosing the river route simply because another vehicle appears to cross successfully. Rain upstream can change water levels, and rental-car insurance may not cover damage caused by driving through rivers.

Do You Need a 4x4 for This Route?

A four-wheel-drive vehicle is not normally required for the standard paved route through Tilarán, Cañas, Liberia, Belén, Huacas and Brasilito. A higher-clearance vehicle can still be more comfortable on occasional rough sections, but it isn’t a requirement for this route the way it would be if you chose to attempt the Monkey Trail instead.

That’s really the core of the decision: it’s less about 4x4 versus 2WD in general, and more about which route you’re taking. The paved route is a standard-vehicle road. Route 911, with its river crossings, is a genuinely different situation — which is exactly why we recommend avoiding it rather than treating it as something a 4x4 makes safe. As noted above, rental-car insurance may not cover damage from driving through rivers, regardless of the vehicle.

One more thing worth checking: the paved route gets you to Playa Flamingo, but the last stretch of road to your specific hotel, villa or rental property can vary. If you’re staying somewhere off the main road, it’s worth asking your accommodation directly whether their access road needs anything beyond a standard vehicle.

How Long Does the Drive Take?

Plan approximately five hours from La Fortuna to Playa Flamingo when using the paved route, without including a long lunch or sightseeing stop.

The section around Lake Arenal is scenic but winding, so average speeds are slower than many international visitors expect. Traffic near Liberia, roadwork and heavy rain can also increase the total driving time.

Leave La Fortuna early enough to complete the trip during daylight. Driving unfamiliar mountain and rural roads after dark is more difficult because of limited lighting, pedestrians, cyclists, animals and changing road conditions.

Should You Keep Your Rental Car or Hire a Driver?

Keeping the same rental car is usually the simplest option for travelers spending two weeks in Costa Rica. It avoids coordinating another rental office, paying possible one-way fees and transferring luggage between vehicles.

Self-driving is reasonable when you are comfortable with winding roads, can leave early and are willing to follow the longer paved route.

A private driver is a better option when the road makes you anxious, you prefer to relax during the transfer, you are traveling with young children or you expect to leave La Fortuna later in the day.

Hiring a driver and renting another car in Playa Flamingo can work, but it usually adds another reservation, vehicle inspection and luggage transfer. Before choosing this option, compare the complete cost with keeping the original rental car.

Do You Need a Car in Playa Flamingo?

A car is useful if you plan to explore Brasilito, Playa Conchal, Potrero, Tamarindo and other Guanacaste beaches independently.

If you plan to remain mainly at your hotel, marina or beach and already have organized excursions, private transportation may be enough. Your decision should depend on how often you expect to leave Playa Flamingo rather than on the transfer day alone.
travel_tip: Add Belén de Carrillo, Huacas and Brasilito as intermediate stops in Waze. Before starting the drive, zoom out and confirm that the route does not send you through Sardinal, Potrero or Route 911.
content_block_faq:
Frequently Asked Questions

What route avoids the Monkey Trail?

Use Route 142 from La Fortuna toward Tilarán and Cañas, Route 1 toward Liberia, Route 21 to Belén, Route 155 to Huacas and Route 180 through Brasilito to Playa Flamingo.

Is the route through Belén and Huacas paved?

It is the standard paved alternative used to avoid the river crossings on Route 911. Temporary construction, potholes or maintenance can still occur, so check current conditions before departure.

Why does Waze recommend Route 911?

Navigation applications often prioritize the shortest estimated travel time. They may not fully reflect a traveler’s comfort with narrow roads, river crossings or driving conditions after rain.

Can I select avoid unpaved roads in Waze?

You can review navigation settings, but the safest method is to add Belén de Carrillo, Huacas and Brasilito as intermediate destinations and inspect the complete route before leaving.

Is Route 911 safe in July?

Conditions vary according to recent rainfall. July is part of the green season, so travelers who are uncomfortable with river crossings should use the paved route rather than depending on the water level that day.

Do I need a four-wheel-drive vehicle for the paved route?

A four-wheel-drive vehicle is not normally required for the standard route through Tilarán, Cañas, Liberia, Belén, Huacas and Brasilito. A higher vehicle can still be more comfortable on occasional rough sections.

Should we hire a private driver instead?

Choose a private driver when you do not feel comfortable with a long, winding drive or prefer not to navigate unfamiliar roads. Otherwise, keeping the same rental car is generally simpler for a two-week trip.

Should we drive this route at night?

We recommend completing the drive during daylight. The Lake Arenal section is winding, and some roads have limited lighting, shoulders and visibility after dark.
content_block_3:
Our Recommendation

If you already have a rental car in La Fortuna and plan to use it during the rest of your two-week vacation, keep the vehicle and take the longer paved route.

Leave early, use Waze for traffic information and add Belén de Carrillo, Huacas and Brasilito as stops. This prevents the application from redirecting you toward the Monkey Trail simply because it appears faster.

Choose a private driver when avoiding the stress of navigation is more important than having the same vehicle throughout the trip. However, hiring a driver and collecting another rental car in Playa Flamingo is not necessary solely to avoid Route 911.

The paved route takes longer, but it provides the more predictable experience most first-time visitors are looking for.
